crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

children.name: Harmonising Privacy Frameworks
children.blurb: Harmonising privacy frameworks in AI practice means aligning obligations across the major data protection regimes, including the GDPR, the UK GDPR, California's CPRA, Brazil's LGPD and China's PIPL, so that a single processing activity can be assessed once against a common control set.

children.name: Incident Response and Breach Notification
children.blurb: Incident response and breach notification in an AI context covers detecting, containing, assessing, and reporting security events that involve personal data or AI systems.

children.name: Cross-Border Data Transfers
children.blurb: Cross-border data transfers in AI work cover the movement of personal data, training data, model outputs, and related metadata from one legal jurisdiction to another.

children.name: AI Supply Chain Liability
children.blurb: AI supply chain liability concerns the allocation of legal responsibility for harm caused by an AI system across the organizations that build, train, integrate, deploy, or use it.

children.name: Biometric and Surveillance Law
children.blurb: Biometric and surveillance law covers the collection, use, retention, and sharing of biometric identifiers such as face, fingerprint, iris, voice, and gait data, along with surveillance technologies like facial recognition, automated license plate readers, and video analytics.

sections.body: Data privacy and cyber-regulatory compliance for AI is the work of fitting machine learning systems into rules about personal data, security, and surveillance. In practice, AI is used to scan data stores, classify records, flag unusual access, triage breach alerts, and score third-party risk. It also powers biometric matching, emotion or gait analysis, and large-scale monitoring, which pushes the same systems into privacy law. The field is not mainly about abstract ethics, it is about notices, consent records, transfer mechanisms, impact assessments, retention limits, and incident logs. Teams now automate data mapping and subject access requests, but the legal judgment about lawful basis and necessity remains human. The compliance question is often whether an AI system can explain what it did with personal data and why.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: The work stands unevenly. Breach notification timelines, privacy impact assessments, and standard contractual clauses are well established in many jurisdictions, so the basic machinery exists. What is not solved is harmonisation, because overlapping national laws, sector rules, and state bills create conflicting duties for the same model or dataset. Cross-border transfers remain fragile when legal challenges invalidate a mechanism, and AI supply chains add another gap because a developer may not know what data a foundation model saw or what a downstream vendor does with outputs. Biometric and surveillance law is a patchwork, with some places banning certain uses and others permitting them under notice or consent. This site tracks 215 compliance and regulation pages and 6940 state AI bills, which shows how much of the field is still being written, and enforcement remains uneven.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: For a reader, Harmonising Privacy Frameworks is the starting point for comparing how different regimes define personal data, lawful basis, and accountability. Incident Response and Breach Notification then covers the operational clock, including detection, containment, assessment, and when regulators or individuals must be told. Cross-Border Data Transfers explains the mechanisms and risks when personal data moves between jurisdictions, which matters for cloud training and global AI services. AI Supply Chain Liability follows the chain from data source to model provider to deployer, and it asks who bears responsibility when a vendor or model causes harm. Biometric and Surveillance Law is the specialised branch for faces, voices, fingerprints, gait, and always-on monitoring, where privacy rules often become stricter. Read together, these pages show that compliance is not one checklist but a set of linked decisions about data, vendors, borders, and sensors.
